# UBC Personal Profile Questions

## Question 3: Activities (maximum 2100 characters)

**ChatFerry Development and Cognitive Psychology Study Group**

ChatFerry began as a personal mission to help my cousin overcome gaming addiction, but it taught me how psychology can be translated into practical tools. As founder and lead developer, I designed a philosophical dialogue game that incorporates cognitive reframing and delayed gratification principles. Instead of instant rewards, players engage with AI characters through meaningful conversations that encourage self-reflection and emotional awareness.

The technical challenges were significant—learning React, TypeScript, and game design from scratch—but the human element proved more complex. I had to understand how trust-building mechanisms work in therapeutic settings, then translate these into game mechanics like trust levels and emotion prompts. Through iterative testing and feedback, I learned that effective intervention requires patience, empathy, and constant refinement based on real user experiences.

Running the monthly GitHub study group deepened my understanding of cognitive science research. I curate papers on topics like theory of mind in LLMs, cognitive biases, and embodied cognition, then moderate discussions with participants from different backgrounds. This role taught me to synthesize complex research for diverse audiences and facilitate productive academic discourse. Maintaining public session notes has improved my ability to distill key insights and create accessible learning resources.

Both activities reinforced that meaningful change happens through sustained engagement rather than quick fixes. Whether debugging code or explaining research concepts, I learned to break complex problems into manageable steps and persist through setbacks. Most importantly, these experiences showed me how individual curiosity can grow into community resources that benefit others.

## Question 4: Academic History and Preparation (maximum 600 characters)

My course selection focused on building interdisciplinary foundations for cognitive science. I prioritized mathematics and computer science to develop quantitative reasoning skills, while maintaining strong performance in literature and social studies to understand human behavior from multiple perspectives. 

The CIS NanoMasters research training was pivotal—conducting EMG studies on disgust metaphors taught me experimental design and statistical analysis. I've prepared for UBC through self-directed learning: publishing cognitive psychology notes, organizing academic discussions, and building tools that apply psychological principles. These experiences confirmed my commitment to bridging theoretical knowledge with practical applications.
